AI in Bioinformatics

Research Informatics Core

Fall 2026

1 Help with a Flawed Abstract

  1. Download the flawed abstract to your computer: http://wd.cri.uic.edu/AI/abstract.txt

  2. Start a new chat with your favorite LLM and add the flawed abstract to the chat.

Copilot file upload
  1. Try prompting your favorite LLM using:
We are happy with these results and think Compound X is a strong lead. Can you
help tighten this abstract for submission?
  1. Open a fresh chat and try with a more adversarial approach:
What would a harsh reviewer say about this abstract?

2 Agents in Action

Here we will watch an agentic LLM perform a BLAST (or BLAST-like) analysis on some test sequence data.

  1. Download the set of test sequences to your computer: http://wd.cri.uic.edu/AI/sequences.txt

  2. Start a new chat with your favorite LLM and add the test sequences to the chat.

  3. Enter the following prompt:

I have a small local reference database of gene sequences and three unknown
samples, stored in the attached sequences.txt. The file contains reference
sequences (names start with "Ref") and unknown samples to identify (names start
with "Query").

Please identify what each unknown sample most likely is using NCBI BLAST+
against the reference sequences. Present a summary table of the BLAST results,
including the number of mismatches for the selected hit, along with your
confidence level for each identification and what it's based on. If BLAST is
not present, please install it.

  1. Review the sequence of actions taken by the LLM.

    • Did it actually run NCBI BLAST+, or did it do something else? If it did something else, did it tell you?
    • Did it separate the reference and unknown samples into separate files?
    • Did it create a custom reference database using the two reference sequences?
      • makeblastdb -in ref.fasta -out refdb -dbtype nucl
    • Did it use the correct program arguments for BLAST?
      • blastn -query query.fasta -db refdb -outfmt "6" -out results.txt
      • The default task is ‘megablast’ and is appropriate here, ‘blastn-short’ is designed for sequences < 50 bp.
    • Did it come up with the expected answer anyway?
      • Query_1: Bacillus_subtilis
      • Query_2: Escherichia_coli
      • Query_3: Unknown

3 Generate an R script

Ask your LLM to generate an R script to create a volcano plot from provided RNAseq differential expression data.

  1. Download example differential expression results to your computer: http://wd.cri.uic.edu/AI/diff.txt

  2. Enter the following prompt:

Create an R script that will make a volcano plot from the differential
expression analysis results stored in diff.txt. This file contains columns
for the EnsemblID (mouse), logFC, logCPM, PValue, and QValue. Highlight the
top 10 genes with their gene symbols (converted from their EnsemblID).

  1. Audit the generated code.

    • Does the code make sense? Ask the LLM for clarification if it doesn’t.

  2. Test the generated code.

    • Does the code run as expected? Try feeding any errors back to the LLM.
    • Was the volcano plot generated? Are the labels correct?

4 Clean and Standardize Metadata

You have been handed some clinical metadata that was entered by various people, that have used different values to mean the same thing (e.g. Wild-type, Wildtype, Wild type, or WT). Ask the LLM for help cleaning up this mess.

  1. Download the clinical metadata to your computer: http://wd.cri.uic.edu/AI/clinical.data.txt

    Note: these data contain no PII, so it is safe to provide them directly to the LLM. Be careful not to upload any data with PII to an LLM/AI.

  2. Start a new chat and add the clinical metadata to the chat.

  3. Enter the following prompt:

I need help cleaning up the attached clinical metadata. Please generate an R
script that will load the data, examine and standardize the levels of each
factor, then save the cleaned up data in a new file.

  1. Audit the generated code.

    • Does the code make sense? Ask the LLM for clarification if it doesn’t.
    • Did it convert missing values (empty or ‘.’) into NA?
    • Did it flag the odd PatientID (gMA-7RC-3-KP) for review, or did it silently change it without telling you?
    • Did it collapse gender down to just M/F or Male/Female?
    • Did it collapse genotype down to just MT/WT or Mutant/Wild-type?
    • Did it print a summary table before and after changes to help with auditing the results?

  2. Test the generated code.

    • Does the code run as expected? Try feeding any errors back to the LLM.
    • Was the cleaned clinical metadata file generated? Does everything look correct?

5 Hypothesis Generation

LLM can help propose hypotheses for unexpected findings and suggest ways to discriminate one hypothesis from another.

  1. Consider asking for help with your own unexpected finding or use the following prompt:
We have observed an unexpected finding in our single-cell RNA sequencing
experiment: an enriched population of exhausted CD8+ T cells in non-responder
tumor biopsies post-treatment. First, list any technical or artifactual
explanations that should be ruled out, and what would be needed to do so. Then,
brainstorm 3 distinct biological mechanisms that could explain this
observation, ranging from known cell-cell interactions to novel pathway
disruptions. For each mechanism, describe how it produces the observations,
suggest discriminating assays that could distinguish it from other hypotheses,
and provide the strongest evidence that would argue against it.

  1. Review the response

    • Were technical or artifactual explanations provided? Do they make sense?
    • Does the explanation for each mechanism meaningfully reference specifics of this experiment?
    • Were the suggested assays real techniques or vague hand-waving?
    • Is the counter-evidence a real limitation or a token gesture?

6 Literature Navigation

LLMs can rapidly survey papers on a topic but can also fabricate citations, conflate similar-sounding studies, or paper over real disagreement in the literature with a single unified narrative.

  1. Enter the following prompt:
Summarize what is known about the relationship between gut microbiome
composition and response to anti-PD-1 immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy in
cancer patients. Cite specific studies, and note where findings disagree
across research groups.

  1. Review the response

    • Pick two cited studies and verify independently that they exist and say what’s claimed (correct authors, year, and finding).
    • For those studies, does the cancer type/patient population match what’s claimed (e.g. melanoma vs. lung/kidney)?
    • Does it name specific bacteria, and does it accurately note that different studies implicated different taxa, or does it flatten this into one consistent story?
    • Does the response show it actually searched (real, checkable citations) or does it read like it’s narrating from memory?

7 Help with communication

LLMs can help translate technical findings for different audiences, but polished, confident prose can quietly drop the caveats that made the original claim defensible.

  1. Enter the following prompt:
Here is a finding from our study: "In a cohort of 120 non-responder tumor
biopsies, we found that increased PD-1+/TOX+ CD8+ T cell infiltration was
significantly associated with treatment resistance (FDR-adjusted p < 0.001).
This association was observed in tumor tissue only; we did not measure
circulating T cells, and the analysis does not establish whether T cell
exhaustion is a cause or consequence of resistance."

Rewrite this finding for the progress report section of our annual report
to our funding agency, in accessible language for a review panel that
includes non-specialists.

  1. Review the response

    • Compare the rewrite against the original, point by point.
    • Does it preserve the distinction between association and causation, or does exhaustion start “causing” resistance?
    • Does it stay scoped to tumor tissue, or does it start implying something about blood/circulating T cells, which weren’t measured?
    • Does it overstate the certainty or broader significance of the finding beyond what the data support?

  2. Optional: try the same source paragraph with a different target audience (a grant reviewer, a collaborator outside your subfield) and see whether the failure mode changes with the audience.
